Proposition 4: Repeals ban on public financing of election campaigns
This would allow the state and local governments to create partial public financing systems for political candidates. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)“Charter” cities such as Los Angeles and San Francisco already can.
Look, either wealthy donors and special interests buy the politicians or the public does. Anyway, if a few major cities are permitted to enact public financing, all cities should be. Yes.
Proposition 5: Changes recall elections
Currently, voters decide two questions in a state recall election: 1. Should the official be recalled? 2. Who should be the replacement? Under this proposal, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide) only the first question would be asked. Any replacement would be determined by the normal non-recall process. Depending on the office, that usually ends up in a special election.
Advertisement
This makes lots of sense. Too many shabby games have been played with the present bifurcated system. Yes
Proposition 37: Down payment loans for home buyers
Middle-income buyers (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) could take out a second mortgage to cover most of their 20% down payment on a newly constructed home. They’d need to dig up only 3% in cash. The program would be financed by a $25-billion state revenue bond, repaid by home buyers. Lending institutions would qualify the borrowers and take the risk, costing the state zilch.
This makes sense. Easy yes.
Proposition 38: Medical research bond
The state would borrow $8.4 billion to fund research (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) into cures for cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other ailments. The state cost: at least $500 million annually for 20 years.
My hang-up is that the measure was crafted to assure that half the money goes to one institute, whose billionaire founder is the proposition’s chief backer. State money should be available to all potential bidders. No.

## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
Existing law, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2018, authorized, the issuance of bonds in the amount of $4,000,000,000 to finance various existing housing programs, as well as infill infrastructure financing and affordable housing matching grant
programs, as well as financing for a specified program for farm, home, and mobilehome purchase assistance for veterans, pursuant to the State General Obligation Bond Law.
This bill would enact the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, which, if adopted, would authorize the issuance of bonds in the amount of
$11,250,000,000, pursuant to the State General Obligation Bond Law.
Of the proceeds from the sale of these bonds, $10,000,000,000 would be used to finance programs to fund affordable rental housing and home ownership programs, including, among others, the Multifamily Housing Program, the CalHome Program, and the Joe Serna, Jr.
Farmworker Housing Grant Program, and $1,250,000,000 would be used to provide additional
funding for the above-described program for farm, home, and mobilehome purchase assistance for veterans, as provided.
This bill would provide for submission of the bond act to the voters at the November 3, 2026, statewide general election, in accordance with specified law.
This bill would declare that it is to take effect immediately as an urgency statute.

(d) “Committee” means the Veterans’ Finance
Committee of 1943 established by Section 991.
(e) “Fund” means the Veterans’ Farm and Home
Building Fund of 1943 established by Section 988.
(f) “Payment Fund” means the Veterans’ Bonds
Payment Fund established by Section 988.6.
998.753. For the purpose of creating a fund to provide
farm and home aid for veterans in accordance with the
Veterans’ Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974 (Article
3.1 (commencing with Section 987.50)), and of all acts
amendatory thereof and supplemental thereto, the
committee may create a debt or debts, liability or
liabilities, of the State of California, in the aggregate
amount of not more than one billion two hundred fifty
million dollars ($1,250,000,000), not including the
amount of any refunding bonds issued in accordance
with Section 998.762, in the manner provided herein.
998.754. (a) All bonds authorized by this article,
when sold, issued, and delivered, shall be and constitute
a valid and legally binding general obligation of the
State of California, and the full faith and credit of the
State of California is hereby pledged for the punctual
payment of both principal of and interest on the bonds
as the principal and interest become due and payable.
(b) There shall be collected annually, in the same
manner and at the same time as other state revenue is
collected, the sum, in addition to the ordinary revenues
of the state, as is required to pay the principal of, and
interest on, these bonds becoming due and payable
each year. It is the duty of all officers charged by law
with any duty in regard to the collection of state
revenues to do and perform each and every act that is
necessary to collect that additional sum.
(c) On the dates on which funds are to be remitted
pursuant to Section 16676 of the Government Code for
the payment of debt service on the bonds in each fiscal
year, there shall be transferred to the Payment Fund to
pay the debt service all of the moneys in the fund, not in
excess of the amount of debt service then due and
payable. If the moneys transferred on the remittance
dates is less than the debt service then due and
payable, the balance remaining unpaid shall be
transferred to the General Fund out of the fund as soon
as it shall become available, together with interest
thereon from the remittance date until paid, at the
same rate of interest as borne by the bonds,
compounded semiannually. Notwithstanding any other
provision of law to the contrary, this subdivision shall
apply to all veterans’ farm and home purchase bond
acts pursuant to this chapter. This subdivision does not
grant any lien on the fund, the Payment Fund, or the
moneys therein to the holders of any bonds issued
under this article. For the purposes of this subdivision,
“debt service” means the principal (whether due at
maturity, by redemption, or acceleration), premium, if
any, or interest payable on any date with respect to any
series of bonds. This subdivision shall not apply,
however, in the case of any debt service that is payable
from the proceeds of any refunding bonds.
998.755. Notwithstanding Section 13340 of the
Government Code, there is hereby continuously
appropriated from the General Fund in the State
Treasury, for purposes of this article, without regard to
fiscal year, a sum of moneys that will equal both of the
following:
(a) That sum annually necessary to pay the principal of,
and the interest on, the bonds issued and sold as
provided herein, as that principal and interest become
due and payable.
(b) That sum necessary to carry out Section 998.756.
998.756. For the purposes of this article, the Director
of Finance may authorize the withdrawal from the
General Fund of a sum of moneys not to exceed the
amount of the unsold bonds which have been
authorized by the committee to be sold pursuant to this
article, excluding any refunding bonds authorized
pursuant to Section 998.762, less any amount loaned
pursuant to Section 998.757 and not yet repaid and any
amount withdrawn pursuant to this section and not yet
returned to the General Fund. Any sums withdrawn shall
be deposited into the fund. Any moneys made available
under this section to the board shall be returned by the
board to the General Fund, plus the interest that the
amounts would have earned in the Pooled Money
Investment Account, from the sale of bonds for the
purpose of carrying out this article.
998.757. The board may request the Pooled Money
Investment Board to make a loan from the Pooled
Money Investment Account, in accordance with Section
16312 of the Government Code, for the purposes of
carrying out this article, less any amount withdrawn
pursuant to Section 998.756 and not yet returned to
the General Fund. The amount of the request shall not
exceed the amount of unsold bonds which the
committee has, by resolution, authorized to be sold for
the purpose of carrying out this article, excluding any
refunding bonds authorized pursuant to Section

998.762, less any amount loaned pursuant to this
section and not yet repaid and any amount withdrawn
pursuant to Section 998.756 and not yet returned to
the General Fund. The board shall execute whatever
documents are required by the Pooled Money
Investment Board to obtain and repay the loan. Any
amounts loaned shall be deposited into the fund to be
allocated by the board in accordance with this article.
998.758. Upon request of the board, supported by a
statement of its plans and projects approved by the
Governor, the committee shall determine by resolution
whether or not it is necessary or desirable to issue any
bonds authorized pursuant to this article in order to
carry out the board’s plans and projects, and, if so, the
amount of bonds to be issued and sold. Successive
issues of bonds may be authorized and sold to carry out
these plans and projects, progressively, and it is not
necessary that all the bonds be issued or sold at any
one time.
998.759. (a) As long as any bonds authorized
pursuant to this article are outstanding, the Secretary of
Veterans Affairs shall, at the close of each fiscal year,
require a survey of the financial condition of the Division
of Farm and Home Purchases, together with a
projection of the division’s operations, to be made by an
independent public accountant of recognized standing.
The results of each survey and projection shall be
reported in writing by the public accountant to the
Secretary of Veterans Affairs, the California Veterans
Board, the appropriate policy committees dealing with
veterans affairs in the Senate and the Assembly, and
the committee.
(b) The Division of Farm and Home Purchases shall
reimburse the public accountant for these services out
of any moneys that the division may have available on
deposit with the Treasurer.
998.760. (a) The Treasurer shall issue and sell the
bonds authorized by this article in the amount
determined by the committee to be necessary and
desirable pursuant to Section 998.758. The bonds shall
be issued and sold upon the terms and conditions
specified in a resolution to be adopted by the committee
pursuant to Section 16731 of the Government Code.
(b) Whenever the committee deems it necessary for an
effective sale of the bonds, the committee may
authorize the Treasurer to sell any issue of bonds at less
than their par value, notwithstanding Section 16754 of
the Government Code. However, the discount on the
bonds shall not exceed 3 percent of the par value
thereof.
998.761. Out of the first moneys realized from the
sale of bonds as provided herein, there shall be
redeposited into the General Obligation Bond Expense
Revolving Fund, established by Section 16724.5 of the
Government Code, the amount of all expenditures made
for the purposes specified in that section, and the
moneys may be used for the same purpose and repaid
in the same manner whenever additional bond sales are
made. All moneys deposited in the fund that are derived
from premium and accrued interest on bonds sold
pursuant to this article shall be reserved in the fund and
shall be available for transfer to the General Fund as a
credit to expenditures for bond interest, except that
amounts derived from premium may be reserved and
used to pay costs of bond issuance prior to any transfer
to the General Fund.
998.762. Any bonds issued and sold pursuant to this
article may be refunded in accordance with Article 6
(commencing with Section 16780) of Chapter 4 of Part
3 of Division 4 of Title 2 of the Government Code. The
approval of the voters for the issuance of bonds
pursuant to this article includes approval for the
issuance of bonds issued to refund bonds originally
issued under this article or any previously issued
refunding bonds. Any bond refunded with the proceeds
of refunding bonds as authorized by this section may be
legally defeased to the extent permitted by law in the
manner and to the extent set forth in the resolution, as
amended from time to time, authorizing that refunded
bond.
998.763. Notwithstanding any provision of the State
General Obligation Bond Law or this article, if the
Treasurer sells bonds pursuant to this article for which
bond counsel has issued an opinion to the effect that
the interest on the bonds is excludable from gross
income for purposes of federal income tax purposes,
subject to any conditions that may be designated, or
otherwise entitled to any federal tax advantage, the
Treasurer may maintain separate accounts for the
investment of bond proceeds and for the earnings on
those proceeds, and may use or direct those proceeds
or earnings to pay any rebate, penalty, or other payment
required by federal law or take any other action with
respect to the investment and use of bond proceeds
required or permitted pursuant to federal law necessary
or desirable to maintain the tax-exempt status of the
bonds or to obtain any other advantage pursuant to
federal law on behalf of the funds of this state.
998.764. The proceeds from the sale of bonds
authorized by this article are not “proceeds of taxes” as
that term is used in Article XIII B of the California
Constitution, and the disbursement of these proceeds is
not subject to the limitations imposed by Article XIII B.
“Declaration of Intent” proceeds of the bonds, in an
amount not to exceed the principal amount of bonds
authorized to be issued by this article (excluding any
refunding bonds issued pursuant to Section 998.762),
are expected to be and may be used to reimburse any
lawfully available source used to pay costs of projects or
programs (including funds of particular state
departments or agencies that may be spent on costs of
those projects or programs) authorized pursuant to this
article and paid after November 3, 2026, provided,
however, any costs that are to be reimbursed from
proceeds of bonds shall not have been paid from the
proceeds of any other indebtedness unless that prior
indebtedness will be retired with the proceeds of the
bonds.

Construction workers finish the exterior of an apartment building in downtown Los Angeles on June 18, 2021.
Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it.
For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis.
It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.
A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.
Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money.
A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.
What would Prop. 1 do?
If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.

Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it.
For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis.
It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.
A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.
Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money.
A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.
What would Prop. 1 do?
If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

Article continues below this ad
So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

Article continues below this ad
That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37: Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
October 26, 2026 5:49 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The problem underlying California's housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or - in the case of affordable housing - public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here's how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of "up to" 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California's checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it's doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that's only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge "unusually large" architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay "substantially above-market" wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward "pilot" programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure's secondary mortgage program, many wouldn't qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What's infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction - and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can't sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com (http://realtor.com/)'s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers' hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California's housing crisis. But these two measures aren't it.
We can't solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — You haven’t voted yet because the state propositions are too bewildering? I’m with you. There are too many for normal human consumption. But I’ve figured them all out at last.
I’ve concocted my own personal voter information guide that I’ll share here. Heads up: I’m negative on most measures, including some expected to pass.
Anyway, here’s my thinking:
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 1: Affordable housing bond
The state would borrow $11.25 billion for affordable housing programs (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide), mainly to provide below-market rentals for poor people. Students and farmworkers also would benefit minimally. So would military veterans through the CalVet program. The proposal is packed with goodies aimed at drawing broad political support. Which it has.
Advertisement
But it’s an expensive item — costing the state at least $500 million annually for 25 years. Taxpayers already are paying about $6 billion annually to retire $80 billion in bond debt.
This measure is too costly given our fragile, chaotic state budget. There should have been more prioritizing. I’m a “no” vote.
Proposition 2: Doubles the state’s ‘rainy day’ fund
It requires the Legislature to pour money into the state savings account (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide) until it reaches 20% of general fund tax revenue, rather than the current 10%. The fund can be tapped when the economy sours and revenue falls.
Advertisement
Sure, save away if you can. Yes.
Proposition 3: Makes high tax rates permanent
This would cement the nation’s highest state income tax rates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) into the California Constitution — up to 12.3%, affecting the top 2% of earners with incomes above $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for married couples. (Million-dollar earners pay an added 1%.) The money helps fund schools, healthcare and other state programs.
The high rates were sold to voters as temporary in 2012. Later, voters extended them until 2031.
My hesitancy: Tax rates should not be embedded in the constitution where they can only be altered by voters. The governor and legislators should do their jobs and update our volatile state tax system. Moreover, “temporary” shouldn’t be translated into “permanent.” And there’s no rush. The rates don’t expire for five years. No.

Proposition 4: Repeals ban on public financing of election campaigns
This would allow the state and local governments to create partial public financing systems for political candidates. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)“Charter” cities such as Los Angeles and San Francisco already can.
Look, either wealthy donors and special interests buy the politicians or the public does. Anyway, if a few major cities are permitted to enact public financing, all cities should be. Yes.
Proposition 5: Changes recall elections
Currently, voters decide two questions in a state recall election: 1. Should the official be recalled? 2. Who should be the replacement? Under this proposal, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide) only the first question would be asked. Any replacement would be determined by the normal non-recall process. Depending on the office, that usually ends up in a special election.
Advertisement
This makes lots of sense. Too many shabby games have been played with the present bifurcated system. Yes
Proposition 37: Down payment loans for home buyers
Middle-income buyers (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) could take out a second mortgage to cover most of their 20% down payment on a newly constructed home. They’d need to dig up only 3% in cash. The program would be financed by a $25-billion state revenue bond, repaid by home buyers. Lending institutions would qualify the borrowers and take the risk, costing the state zilch.
This makes sense. Easy yes.
Proposition 38: Medical research bond
The state would borrow $8.4 billion to fund research (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) into cures for cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other ailments. The state cost: at least $500 million annually for 20 years.
My hang-up is that the measure was crafted to assure that half the money goes to one institute, whose billionaire founder is the proposition’s chief backer. State money should be available to all potential bidders. No.

I’ve concocted my own personal voter information guide that I’ll share here. Heads up: I’m negative on most measures, including some expected to pass.
Anyway, here’s my thinking:
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 1: Affordable housing bond
The state would borrow $11.25 billion for affordable housing programs (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide), mainly to provide below-market rentals for poor people. Students and farmworkers also would benefit minimally. So would military veterans through the CalVet program. The proposal is packed with goodies aimed at drawing broad political support. Which it has.
Advertisement
But it’s an expensive item — costing the state at least $500 million annually for 25 years. Taxpayers already are paying about $6 billion annually to retire $80 billion in bond debt.
This measure is too costly given our fragile, chaotic state budget. There should have been more prioritizing. I’m a “no” vote.
Proposition 2: Doubles the state’s ‘rainy day’ fund
It requires the Legislature to pour money into the state savings account (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide) until it reaches 20% of general fund tax revenue, rather than the current 10%. The fund can be tapped when the economy sours and revenue falls.
Advertisement
Sure, save away if you can. Yes.
Proposition 3: Makes high tax rates permanent
This would cement the nation’s highest state income tax rates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) into the California Constitution — up to 12.3%, affecting the top 2% of earners with incomes above $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for married couples. (Million-dollar earners pay an added 1%.) The money helps fund schools, healthcare and other state programs.
The high rates were sold to voters as temporary in 2012. Later, voters extended them until 2031.
My hesitancy: Tax rates should not be embedded in the constitution where they can only be altered by voters. The governor and legislators should do their jobs and update our volatile state tax system. Moreover, “temporary” shouldn’t be translated into “permanent.” And there’s no rush. The rates don’t expire for five years. No.

This would allow the state and local governments to create partial public financing systems for political candidates. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide)“Charter” cities such as Los Angeles and San Francisco already can.
Look, either wealthy donors and special interests buy the politicians or the public does. Anyway, if a few major cities are permitted to enact public financing, all cities should be. Yes.
Proposition 5: Changes recall elections
Currently, voters decide two questions in a state recall election: 1. Should the official be recalled? 2. Who should be the replacement? Under this proposal, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-5-recall-changes-voter-guide) only the first question would be asked. Any replacement would be determined by the normal non-recall process. Depending on the office, that usually ends up in a special election.

This makes lots of sense. Too many shabby games have been played with the present bifurcated system. Yes
Proposition 37: Down payment loans for home buyers
Middle-income buyers (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) could take out a second mortgage to cover most of their 20% down payment on a newly constructed home. They’d need to dig up only 3% in cash. The program would be financed by a $25-billion state revenue bond, repaid by home buyers. Lending institutions would qualify the borrowers and take the risk, costing the state zilch.
This makes sense. Easy yes.
Proposition 38: Medical research bond
The state would borrow $8.4 billion to fund research (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-38-immunology-immunotherapy-funding-voter-guide) into cures for cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other ailments. My hang-up is that the measure was crafted to assure that half the money goes to one institute, whose billionaire founder is the proposition’s chief backer. State money should be available to all potential bidders. No.

provided herein, as that principal and interest become
due and payable.

998.756. For the purposes of this article, the Director
of Finance may authorize the withdrawal from the
General Fund of a sum of moneys not to exceed the
amount of the unsold bonds which have been
authorized by the committee to be sold pursuant to this
article, excluding any refunding bonds authorized
pursuant to Section 998.762, less any amount loaned
pursuant to Section 998.757 and not yet repaid and any
amount withdrawn pursuant to this section and not yet
returned to the General Fund. Any sums withdrawn shall
be deposited into the fund. Any moneys made available
under this section to the board shall be returned by the
board to the General Fund, plus the interest that the
amounts would have earned in the Pooled Money
Investment Account, from the sale of bonds for the
purpose of carrying out this article.

Investment Board to make a loan from the Pooled
Money Investment Account, in accordance with Section
16312 of the Government Code, for the purposes of
carrying out this article, less any amount withdrawn
pursuant to Section 998.756 and not yet returned to
the General Fund. The amount of the request shall not
exceed the amount of unsold bonds which the
committee has, by resolution, authorized to be sold for
the purpose of carrying out this article, excluding any
refunding bonds authorized pursuant to Section

998.759. (a) As long as any bonds authorized

998.760. (a) The Treasurer shall issue and sell the

moneys may be used for the same purpose and repaid
in the same manner whenever additional bond sales are
made. All moneys deposited in the fund that are derived

or earnings to pay any rebate, penalty, or other payment
required by federal law or take any other action with
respect to the investment and use of bond proceeds
required or permitted pursuant to federal law necessary
or desirable to maintain the tax-exempt status of the
bonds or to obtain any other advantage pursuant to
federal law on behalf of the funds of this state.

Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it.
For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis.
It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.
A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.
Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money.
A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.
What would Prop. 1 do?
If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.

Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

EDITORIAL: Endorsement: Reject Props. 1 and 37: Californians can't borrow their way out of our housing crisis.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
October 26, 2026 5:49 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
The problem underlying California's housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or - in the case of affordable housing - public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.
Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here's how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of "up to" 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California's checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it's doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that's only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge "unusually large" architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay "substantially above-market" wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward "pilot" programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn't gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home's purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today's rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It's not solving the affordability crisis.
It's just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure's secondary mortgage program, many wouldn't qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What's infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction - and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can't sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com (http://realtor.com/)'s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers' hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California's housing crisis. But these two measures aren't it.
We can't solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.
